claims.text: Untreated, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer is predominantly composed of iron oxides such as Fe3O4 and Fe2O3.
At approximately 25°C, the intact native oxide limits electron transfer and suppresses corrosion.
At approximately 80°C, the native oxide undergoes structural destabilization, such as microcracking or phase changes.
Elevated-temperature destabilization of the native oxide produces localized galvanic cells.
The localized galvanic cells accelerate localized corrosion.
Removing the native oxide eliminates the proposed temperature-dependent oxide transformations.
Removing the native oxide yields more uniform corrosion kinetics across temperatures.
At room temperature, as-received samples will have lower corrosion current densities than polished samples.
At elevated temperature, as-received samples will exhibit more localized corrosion and accelerated degradation due to oxide destabilization.
At elevated temperature, polished samples will exhibit more uniform corrosion and less pronounced temperature sensitivity than as-received samples.
The proposed controlled study compares mechanically polished and as-received Q235 samples under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
The proposed exposure conditions are 3.5 wt% NaCl at approximately pH 3, 25°C or 80°C, for 24 or 72 hours with controlled flow and oxygen conditions.
Oxide reformation on polished surfaces before or during testing could alter differences between polished and as-received samples.
Variability in native-oxide composition and microstructure among as-received samples could introduce scatter in corrosion measurements.
Statistically indistinguishable corrosion behavior between polished and as-received samples at both temperatures would falsify the proposed oxide-mediated effect.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field treats statistically identical corrosion behavior across both temperatures as decisive falsification, whereas the dedicated falsification rule additionally requires in-situ monitoring to show no significant difference in oxide behavior. Thus, the necessary falsification conditions are stated inconsistently.
